extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP policymakers, and students of patent law (particularly biotechnology/patentable subject-matter under US law)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for determining whether a biotechnology invention (specifically a human-made microorganism) falls within the categories of patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101. Summarizes the Supreme Court's reasoning in Diamond v. Chakrabarty and related interpretive points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 101 statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 101: 'Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comprehensive 'any' together with the listed categories is interpreted to aim at a large scope of patent law; an invention must fall into one of these categories to be patentable subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture — scope and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Manufacture' is taken to mean 'the production of articles for use from raw or prepared materials by giving to these materials new forms, qualities, properties, or combinations, whether by hand-labor or by machinery' (American Fruit Growers, Inc. v. Brodgex Co.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'manufacture' is defined broadly, human-made products (including potentially living things) that exhibit new forms/qualities/properties can fall within this category for §101 purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter — scope and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Composition of matter' is taken to include 'all compositions of two or more substances and… all composite articles, whether they be the results of chemical union, or of mechanical mixture, or whether they be gases, fluids, powders or solids.' (Shell Development Co. v. Watson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novel composition (including engineered biological compositions) can qualify as patentable subject-matter under §101 when it is not merely a naturally occurring substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature vs. human-made invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The significant inquiry is whether an item is a product of nature or a human-made invention; whether something is 'alive' is legally irrelevant to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-naturally occurring, human-made entities qualify for §101 protection as 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter'; naturally occurring phenomena remain excluded (see Funk Brothers and later Myriad/Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of human-made microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: A live, human-made microorganism is patentable subject-matter under §101 and can constitute a 'manufacture' or 'composition of matter' (holding of Diamond v. Chakrabarty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Chakrabarty bacterium (Pseudomonas putida engineered to metabolize hydrocarbons) was held to be non-naturally occurring and the product of human ingenuity, thus patentable; patent claims to such organisms can be allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of claims by category (process, inoculum, organism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim types can be treated differently: process claims and claims to an inoculum/composition were allowed by the examiner, whereas claims to the organism itself were initially rejected as non‑§101 subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafters should note that claim drafting strategy matters: process and composition claims may avoid §101 rejections even where organism claims are contested, but organisms that are shown to be human-made/non-natural can also be patentable as held in Chakrabarty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits: natural phenomena and isolated natural products remain unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent case law confirmed the non-patentability of natural substances such as isolated DNA (Myriad) and natural phenomena (Mayo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even after Chakrabarty's broad interpretation of 'manufacture' and 'composition of matter,' courts continue to exclude mere discoveries of natural phenomena or naturally occurring substances (or their unaltered isolations) from §101 protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory interpretation for new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that genetic technology was unforeseen when Congress enacted §101 does not preclude applying the statute; courts use established interpretive methods (legislative history and statutory purpose) to apply existing law to new matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel technologies are assessed under existing statutory categories through traditional interpretive tools rather than requiring express congressional authorization for each new technological field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant statutes do not imply a categorical exclusion of bacteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of the Plant Patent Act and the Plant Variety Protection Act (which address certain asexually reproduced plants and plant variety protection) does not mean §101 excludes bacteria or other living things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction in plant statutes is between products of nature and human-made inventions and is influenced by considerations like true‑to‑type reproduction; these statutes should not be read as an implicit §101 exclusion for bacteria.
